procedure well and left the department in good condition.

Interpretation of PCT results:
Procalcitonin (PCT) assay is intended to aid in the risk assessment
of critically ill patients.
PCT < 0.5 ng/ml: is associated with a low risk for progression to
severe sepsis and/or septic shock.
PCT levels between 0.5 and 2.0 ng/ml should be interpreted in the
context of the specific clinical background and condition of the
individual patient. It is recommended to retest PCT within 6 - 24
hours if any concentrations of < 2.0 ng/ml are obtained.
PCT > 2.0 ng/ml: is associated with a high risk for progression to
severe sepsis and/or shock.
Note: PCT levels of < 0.5 ng/ml do not exclude an infection,
because localized infections (without systemic signs) may also be
associated with such low levels. If the PCT measurement is done
very early after the systemic infection process has started
(usually < 6 hours), these values may still be low.

associated with slight elevations (metanephrine less than 400 ug/d
and normetanephrine less than 900 ug/d). Elevated concentrations
may be due to intense physical activity, life-threatening illness,
and drug interferences.
Significant elevation of one or both metanephrines (three or more

Strongly Positive OD= greater or equal to 1.000
This ELISA assay detects IgG antibodies against complexes of
heparin and platelet factor 4 (PF4) that are associated with
Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT). An OD >=0.4 is
considered an initial positive, and further testing for
inhibition by heparin is performed. Heparin inhibition by >
or = 50% is a positive result. For proper assessment, the
result would be correlated with the 4Ts clinical scoring
system or other clinical assessment. A higher OD may
represent antibodies capable of platelet activation,
correlating with strong positive serotonin-release assay
results when the screening OD was >1.40. The test is not a
functional assay, and the serotonin release assay may be
useful for additional investigation of HIT.
Assess clinical risk for HIT with the 4T's Scoring System -
score each category; add all points to determine maximum
score (maximum possible score = 8 points)
a. Pretest probability :
low <= 3 points;
intermediate 4 - 5 points;
high 6 - 8 points
i. Thrombocytopenia
1. 0 points = <30% fall or nadir <10x10 to the 9th
power/L
2. 1 point = 30-50% fall or nadir 10x10 to the 9th
power/L - 19x10 to the 9th power/L
3. 2 points = >50% fall and nadir 20-100x10 to the 9th
power/L
ii. Timing of platelet fall count
1. 0 points = <4 days without recent exposure
2. 1 point = consistent with day 5-10 (but not clear),
or >10 days, or <=1 day
(with heparin 30-100 days prior)
3. 2 points = day 5-10 or <=1 day if recent heparin
(within 30 days)
iii. Thrombosis
1. 0 points = none
2. 1 point = progressive, recurrent or silent thromboses
3. 2 points = proven thrombosis; skin necrosis; acute
systemic reaction with heparin bolus
iv. Other causes for thrombocytopenia
1. 0 points = definite
2. 1 point = possible
3. 2 points = none evident
References:
1. Smock KJ.Rodgers GM. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia:
how lab results contribute to clinicopathologic diagnosis.
Clinical Laboratory News May 2009:8-10.
2. Lo GK, Juhl D, Warkentin TE, et al. Evaluation of
pretest clinical score (4T's) for the diagnosis of
heparin-induced thrombocytopenia in two clinical settings.
J Thromb Haemost 2006;4:759-65.
3. Warkentin TE, Sheppard JC, Moore CS, et al. Quantitative
interpretation of optical density measurements using
PFT-dependent enzyme-immunoassays.
J Thromb Haemost 2008;6:1304-12.
4. Refaai MA, Laposata M, Van Cott EM. Clinical
significance of a borderline titer in a vegetative ELISA
test for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
Am J Clin Pathol 2003;119:61-65.
5. Refaai MA, Van Cott, EM, Laposata M. The timing of a
positive test result for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
relative to the platelet count and anticoagulant therapy in
43 consecutive cases. Am J Clin Pathol 2003;119:497-504.
